title: One Granth for all
hook: every stream bows to the same Guru Granth Sahib

segments.voice: Yesterday, many voices: no single head, and a true sangat known by the Name. Your line was many voices, one guru.

Go back over the streams this block has visited. A Nihang camp, blue robes and steel. An Udasi dera with its quiet ascetics. A Nirmala house of learning. A taksal where students drill every vowel. A Namdhari gathering in white. A sangat in New Mexico or Toronto singing in a mix of Punjabi and English. Different clothes, different tunes, different arguments. Now look at the front of each room. Raised a little, under a canopy, wrapped in cloth: the same book. Today is that book, at the center of the streams.
screen: `BLUE ROBES, WHITE CLOTHES, NEW TUNES.` → `LOOK AT THE FRONT OF THE ROOM.` → `THE SAME BOOK.`

segments.voice: The Guru Granth Sahib holds the hymns of Sikh Gurus alongside saints from other backgrounds, Kabir, Ravidas, Farid and more, gathered into one volume and sung in ragas. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh gave it the Guruship. Since then it is not treated as a book on a shelf: it is installed each morning under a canopy, read aloud, waved over with a whisk, and laid to rest at night. When one stream disagrees with another about diet, music, dress or the Dasam Granth, this is where both sides return. They bow to the same Guru. Gurbani gives the reason in Guru Ram Das's words on Ang 982, here in paraphrase: the Word is the Guru, and the Guru is the Word; within the Word are all the nectars. The Guru is not a person anyone can claim for their side. It is the Word itself, open on the same pages in every gurdwara. That has a practical effect. A Sikh walking into a gurdwara of a different stream, in another country, will find the same hymns and the same order of pages, and can sit down and follow along. The Namdharis, too, who keep a living guru of their own, bow before the Guru Granth Sahib and sing from it. The streams are many. The center is one book, and in each of those rooms, heads bow before it.
screen: `GURUS AND SAINTS IN ONE VOLUME.` · `INSTALLED, READ, LAID TO REST.` · `THE WORD IS THE GURU.` · `THE SAME PAGES IN EVERY GURDWARA.` · then, large: `ONE GRANTH FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: If you're near a gurdwara, you can go in, cover your head, and bow before the Guru Granth Sahib; if not, picture the book under its canopy and lower your head a little where you sit. If you don't keep this faith, simply hold respect for a book people of many streams bow to; if you pray, rest on the Word, the Guru.
One Granth for all. Every stream of the panth bows to the same Guru Granth Sahib, the Word as Guru, open on the same pages in every gurdwara. Today's word.
Your line: one granth. The same pages lie open in every room, whatever the stream. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Across the Sikh streams the Guru Granth Sahib is installed under a canopy, read aloud and bowed to as Guru; Sikhs from any stream can follow the same hymns on the same pages in any gurdwara.

chat.says: Nihangs and Namdharis look so different. Do they even read the same scripture?
options: Yes. Every stream bows to the same Guru Granth Sahib, with the same hymns in the same order.
No. Each stream wrote its own Granth, so the hymns change from group to group.
Only in Punjab. Abroad, each sangat writes new hymns to replace the old ones.

Namdharis described as keeping a living guru while bowing before the Guru Granth Sahib and singing from it. Please confirm this is fair to Namdhari self-description and to mainstream Sikh bodies.
Hook lists streams from earlier in Block F, plus Western sangats 'in New Mexico or Toronto'; please confirm these place names are apt.
'The same order of pages in every gurdwara' assumes the standard pagination of printed saroops. Please confirm; the 'so many different people' line in the practice is a soft phrase, not a statistic.
